headline: Your growth plates
punch: And the experiment that proved it is 20 years old.

headline: Everyone treats fusion
body: Stay open longer, beat the clock, get taller. That's what basically every height protocol is built on. The cause and effect is backwards, and once you see why, a lot of advice stops making sense.
punch: Fusion is not what stops you.

headline: The experiment
body: They transplanted growth plates between animals of different ages. If your body set the growth rate, a transplanted plate would grow at the recipient's pace. It didn't. Young plate in an old animal grew fast. Old plate in a young animal stayed slow.
punch: Growth rate followed the donor, every single time.

headline: So the clock
body: It's inside the plate itself. Not your hormones, not your age, not some signal from your brain telling your bones to quit. The plate carries its own history and that history is what runs out.
punch: The plate keeps its own score.

headline: What actually runs out
body: Resting zone chondrocytes have a finite replicative capacity. Every division spends a bit of it. Once the pool is depleted, columns thin out, growth slows, and the plate ossifies.
punch: It's a bank account, not a timer. Nothing refills it.

headline: Which is why growth slows
body: Deceleration comes first. Fusion follows it, sometimes way later.
punch: The closed plate on your X-ray is the receipt for capacity you already spent.

headline: Here's the part
body: Suppress growth for a while and plates grow faster than expected afterwards. Catch-up growth. If fusion ran on a clock, lost time would be gone forever.
punch: Slowing down the division rate saves the account instead of draining it.

headline: So the real target
body: It's preserving proliferative capacity. Those sound like the same thing and they're not. Mixing them up is why so much height advice chases the wrong number.
punch: Chasing a date instead of the thing that sets the date.

headline: And honestly
body: Four competing theories for how fusion actually happens in the cell: apoptosis, autophagy, hypoxia, transdifferentiation. None confirmed in humans. One human study found no classical apoptosis at all.
punch: Anyone certain about this hasn't read the papers.
